title: What’s Behind the Declining Trend Unemployment Rate? - San Francisco Fed
gist: SF Fed researchers estimate that the U.S. trend (cycle-adjusted) unemployment rate fell from 7.8% in 1976 to 4.8% in 2024, with slightly more than half of the 3.3pp drop explained by workforce composition — rising education (-1.1pp) and aging (-0.7pp) — and the rest by successively later birth cohorts carrying structurally lower unemployment propensity. They project a further 0.4pp decline to roughly 4.4% by 2044, implying the level of unemployment that signals a 'tight' labor market keeps drifting lower.

insights.claim: The cycle-adjusted U.S. trend unemployment rate fell from 7.8% in 1976 to 4.8% in 2024, a cumulative decline of about 3.3 percentage points, estimated from 1976–2024 Current Population Survey data.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
insights.so_what: The anchor for judging labor-market slack has moved: a 4.8% print in 2024 is roughly neutral, not loose, versus a 7.8% neutral level in the 1970s.
insights.quote: The total decline was about 3.3 percentage points by 2024.
insights.locator: What drove the decline?

insights.claim: The authors project trend unemployment to decline a further 0.4 percentage point over 20 years, from roughly 4.8% in 2024 to about 4.4% by 2044, purely from projected demographic and educational composition.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: A structurally falling natural rate means each future cycle's 'full employment' unemployment print should be lower — relevant to how the Fed reads NAIRU-style gaps and to long-run rate expectations.
insights.locator: Looking ahead

insights.claim: The estimated trend declines smoothly across five decades while actual unemployment swings widely around it, so the long-run downtrend is structural and demographic rather than an artifact of unusually long expansions.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Argues against reading the low unemployment of recent cycles as pure cyclical overheating — a chunk of it was always going to happen.
insights.quote: the decline in unemployment is not just a cyclical phenomenon: It reflects slow-moving structural and demographic forces.
insights.locator: Figure 1 shows the resulting estimated trend

insights.claim: Estimating the trend correctly is presented as a prerequisite for interpreting any unemployment reading, because the same headline rate signals different degrees of labor-market health depending on the underlying trend.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Frames every unemployment release as a gap-to-trend problem, not a level problem — the input that actually drives policy reaction functions.
insights.quote: Properly assessing this trend is crucial for understanding what a given level of unemployment signals about the health of the labor market.
insights.locator: Underlying the well-known cyclical swings

insights.claim: Slightly more than half of the 3.3pp decline in trend unemployment since 1976 comes from shifts in workforce composition, and the remainder from lower unemployment within demographic groups.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Splits the story roughly 50/50 — demographics alone cannot explain the full drop, so behavioral or structural labor-market change matters too.
insights.quote: Roughly half of that decline reflects compositional change.
insights.locator: We find that the trend unemployment rate declined

insights.claim: Rising educational attainment is the single largest force lowering trend unemployment, worth about 1.1 percentage points, ahead of population aging at roughly 0.7 percentage point.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Education, not aging, is the dominant compositional driver — so a plateau in college attainment would matter more for the trend than demographic tailwinds do.
insights.quote: Rising educational attainment is the single largest compositional force, lowering the trend about 1.1 percentage points.
insights.locator: What drove the decline?

insights.claim: Changes in group-specific trend labor force participation rates contribute only about 0.3 percentage point to the decline in trend unemployment, a much smaller channel than either education or aging.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Participation shifts are largely a red herring for the unemployment trend even though they dominate discussion of labor supply.
insights.locator: What drove the decline?

insights.claim: The remaining decline of a bit under 1 percentage point comes from lower group-specific trend unemployment — the same worker profile (age, gender, education) now faces lower structural unemployment than decades ago.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: A residual worth watching: it is the piece most likely to reverse if labor-market matching or job stability deteriorates.
insights.locator: What drove the decline?

insights.claim: The within-group decline in unemployment comes mainly from newer birth cohorts entering the labor force with lower unemployment propensity, not from every age group facing a uniformly lower structural rate than the same age decades earlier.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: If the improvement is cohort-locked rather than age-based, the tailwind persists mechanically as older cohorts retire — it does not depend on the current cycle.
insights.quote: Rather, newer cohorts appear to be bringing somewhat lower unemployment risk into the labor market.
insights.locator: Cohort and age effects in group-specific unemployment trends

insights.claim: Men's trend unemployment begins edging down in the early 1990s while women's declines more clearly only around 2000, with college-educated women the exception whose decline starts earlier.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Dates the structural improvement to the post-1990 era, which constrains which explanations (trade, technology, education) can plausibly be responsible.
insights.quote: men’s trend unemployment begins to edge down in the early 1990s, while women’s trend unemployment declines more clearly around 2000
insights.locator: Figure 3 shows that the long-run decline

insights.claim: Within-group trend unemployment falls somewhat more for men than for women, but the authors explicitly downplay the gender split as secondary to the aggregate composition story.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Avoids over-reading gender narratives; the actionable variable is education and age mix, not the male/female gap.
insights.quote: The gender comparison is informative, but it is not the main aggregate story.
insights.locator: The gender comparison is informative

themes.theme: Scale of the demographic and education shift

insights.claim: The population share aged 16–24 fell from 22.0% in 1976–1984 to 14.7% in 2016–2024, while the share aged 55 and older rose from 27.3% to 36.6% over the same subperiods.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Quantifies the shrinking share of the highest-unemployment cohort — a mechanical, forecastable downward pull on the headline rate.
insights.locator: These contributions line up with large changes

insights.claim: Among prime-age adults 25–54, the share with more than a high school education rose from 21.0% to 31.9% between the 1976–1984 and 2016–2024 averages, while the share with high school or less fell from 29.8% to 16.8%.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: The low-education prime-age population nearly halved as a population share — the group most exposed to cyclical layoffs is structurally smaller.
insights.locator: These contributions line up with large changes

insights.claim: Educational upgrading is even more dramatic among older workers: the share of people aged 55 and older with more than a high school education rose from 6.0% to 21.3% between the two subperiods.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Aging and education compound rather than offset — the growing older cohort is also increasingly the low-unemployment educated kind.
insights.locator: These contributions line up with large changes

insights.claim: For entering cohorts of women the college share rises from under 10% to roughly 50%, while for men the share with less than high school falls from around 70% for cohorts born in the late 1920s to single digits, with the college share rising from about 10% to nearly 40%.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Shows how much of the education tailwind is already exhausted at the low end — the sub-high-school share cannot fall much further, capping future compositional gains.
insights.quote: For women, the college share rises from less than 10% to roughly 50% for recent cohorts.
insights.locator: Educational upgrading of entering cohorts

insights.claim: Women's educational gains continue later into the sample than men's, consistent with the stronger rise in female educational attainment documented in the authors' companion work on gender divergence in labor force participation.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Female education is the part of the compositional tailwind with the most runway left, making it the marginal driver of the projected 2044 trend.
insights.locator: Educational upgrading of entering cohorts

insights.claim: The estimate is built bottom-up from 44 groups defined by the intersection of two genders, four education categories, and seven age categories, each decomposed into cyclical and trend components and reweighted by population and participation shares.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: A reusable template for separating demographic drift from genuine cyclical signal in any aggregate labor series.
insights.locator: From group trends to aggregate unemployment

insights.claim: Allowing age effects to vary by calendar year — rather than fixing the unemployment rate at a given age across five decades — lets the model capture structural shifts in how labor demand treats a given education level over time.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: This flexibility is what allows the model to attribute part of the decline to cohorts rather than mechanically to aging — the key identifying assumption to scrutinize.
insights.quote: Allowing age effects to vary over time means that unemployment at a given age can shift structurally, rather than being forced to remain fixed for a specific age over the five decades in our sample.
insights.locator: Our procedure creates a time-varying trend estimate

insights.claim: Aging pushes overall labor force participation down while simultaneously pushing overall unemployment down, because older workers who stay in the labor force have lower unemployment rates.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: Explains why falling participation and falling unemployment can coexist without either being a sign of a broken labor market — a common misreading of jobs data.
insights.quote: Aging tends to lower overall LFP because older people participate less, but the same aging process can lower overall unemployment because older workers who remain in the labor force tend to have lower unemployment rates.
insights.locator: Looking ahead

insights.claim: The forecast splices group-specific trend estimates onto U.S. Census Bureau 2023 age-gender population projections plus a cohort state-space model for education shares, so the 4.4% 2044 figure inherits the uncertainty of those two external projections.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hornstein
insights.so_what: The projection is only as good as Census immigration and fertility assumptions — a reason to treat the 4.4% as a central case, not a hard floor.
insights.locator: To generate forecasts of the aggregate trend

top_entities: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
